items.title: Measurement models and additive-error observation models
items.statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), and fix integers $m,d\ge1$.

**Measurement model.** A **measurement model** with input dimension $m$ and
output dimension $d$ consists of

1. an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, the **input domain**, and a map
   $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$, the **model function**, which is Borel measurable as a
   map of measurable spaces
   $$f:(U,\mathcal B(U))\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^d,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d))$$
   ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]],
   [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]);
2. a random element $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, the **input vector**, whose
   values lie in $U$, that is, $X(\omega)\in U$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$
   ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], with target
   $(\mathbb R^m,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m))$);
3. the **output quantity** $Y:=f\circ X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$.

A point $\mu\in U$ is a **nominal input** of the model. The model function is
**continuous**, of class $C^k$, or **totally differentiable at $\mu$** when
$f$ has the corresponding property as a map on the open set $U$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]); such a regularity hypothesis
must be stated whenever a derivative of $f$ is used. The *linearization of
$f$ at $\mu$* is the affine map
$$T_\mu(x):=f(\mu)+Df(\mu)(x-\mu)$$
when $Df(\mu)$ exists.

**Additive-error observation model.** Let $\Theta$ be a set, the **parameter
set**; let $Z$ be a set, the **apparatus and preparation settings**; let
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an open set with $0\in V$, the **error domain**;
let $h:\Theta\times Z\to\mathbb R^d$ be a map, the **prediction map**; and let
$\varepsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with
$\varepsilon(\omega)\in V$ for every $\omega$, the **error**. For each
$(\theta,z)\in\Theta\times Z$ the **observation** is the random element
$$Y_{\theta,z}:=h(\theta,z)+\varepsilon:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^d .$$
Well-definedness: for fixed $\theta$ and $z$ the map
$\tau_{\theta,z}(x):=h(\theta,z)+x$ is a translate of $\mathbb R^m$, hence
continuous, so $\tau_{\theta,z}^{-1}(B)$ is Borel for every Borel
$B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ ([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]);
therefore
$Y_{\theta,z}^{-1}(B)=\varepsilon^{-1}\bigl(\tau_{\theta,z}^{-1}(B)\bigr)\in\mathfrak F$
by the measurability of $\varepsilon$, so $Y_{\theta,z}$ is a random element
in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]].

### Conventions, hypotheses and scope

The following are **additional hypotheses** and are not part of either
definition: that the error has mean zero, $E[\varepsilon]=0$; that
$\varepsilon$ is square-integrable, $E|\varepsilon|^2<+\infty$; that the
error is bounded; that a stated probability law for $\varepsilon$ is
specified; or that the input vector is of the additive form
$X=\mu+\varepsilon$ with a deterministic nominal input $\mu$. Any of these
must be stated, with its exact quantifiers, at each use.

When a model function is merely continuous, continuity and
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]] show that its preimages
of Borel sets are Borel, so clause 1 holds automatically for such $f$; the
explicit measurability in clause 1 keeps the definition meaningful for
discontinuous model functions as well, where required.

The model is an input–output relation between random quantities and their
images. It contains no unit assignment, no physical identification of
$\Theta$, $Z$ or $U$ with measured quantities, no sampling protocol and no
distributional assumption beyond the stated probability space. A physical
consumer must supply the units of the coordinates, the preparation and
apparatus protocol, and the empirical status of every distributional or
moment hypothesis that it invokes.

items.title: Calibration data and calibration rules
items.statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A **calibration
family** is a family
$$\bigl(h_c\bigr)_{c\in C},\qquad h_c:\Theta\longrightarrow\mathbb R^d,$$
of prediction maps on a nonempty parameter set $\Theta$, indexed by a
nonempty set $C$ of **apparatus settings** ([[def-cm-measurement-model]]).

A **calibration datum** for this family consists of

1. a finite family $(\theta^{(r)})_{r<n}$, $n\ge1$, of **reference inputs**
   $\theta^{(r)}\in\Theta$, values supplied by a reference standard under
   stated conditions;
2. a set $Y\subseteq(\mathbb R^d)^n$ of admissible **reference observations**
   and the observed vector $y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)\in Y$;
3. a **calibration rule**, that is, a map
   $$\Gamma:Y\longrightarrow C,\qquad y\longmapsto c;$$
4. either a stated bound $|\theta^{(r)}-\theta^{(r)}_{\mathrm{ref}}|\le\delta_r$
   for the deviation of each reference input from its nominal value, or a
   random element $\eta:\Omega\to\Theta^n$ of deviations with a stated law, so
   that the reference inputs are the random values
   $\theta^{(r)}_{\mathrm{ref}}+\eta_r$.

Given the datum, the **calibrated setting** is $c:=\Gamma(y)$ and the
**calibrated prediction map** is $h_c$.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The rule $\Gamma$ and the sets $C$, $\Theta$, $Y$ are data: nothing in the
definition requires $\Gamma$ to be injective, continuous, measurable, or to
return an apparatus setting for which the calibrated prediction is accurate.
The reference inputs are values of a physical standard; their uncertainty is
recorded in clause 4 and must be carried into any quantitative conclusion
about $h_c$ by the argument that uses it. The definition states the structure
of a calibration only; properties such as consistency, unbiasedness or
attainment of a stated accuracy require separate hypotheses and proofs, and
no such property is asserted here.

items.title: Repeated-observation sampling models with IID and finite-variance hypotheses
items.statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]) and let $n\ge1$ be a natural number. A
**repeated-observation sampling model** for a real quantity consists of random
variables
$$Y_0,\dots,Y_{n-1}:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$
([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]) together with the following
model hypotheses, each of which is adopted as part of the model and is not a
consequence of the data:

1. **(IID hypothesis)** the family $(Y_k)_{k<n}$ is independent and
   identically distributed in the sense of
   [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]; that is, the
   whole family is mutually independent and the laws of the $Y_k$ all agree;
2. **(second-moment hypothesis)** $E\bigl[Y_0^2\bigr]<+\infty$.

Under hypotheses 1 and 2 the numbers
$$\mu:=E[Y_0]\in\mathbb R,\qquad \sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_0)\in[0,+\infty)$$
are finite by [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]], and hypothesis 1 makes
them the common mean and variance of the family; in particular
$E[Y_k]=\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y_k)=\sigma^2$ for every $k<n$. The
**sample mean** of the model is the random variable
$$\overline Y:=\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}Y_k .$$

### Conventions and scope

The data of the model are the probability space, the variables $Y_k$, and the
adopted hypotheses; hypotheses 1 and 2 can fail for the same family of
variables on the same probability space, so they must be stated, not inferred
from the notation. The definition assumes no particular law for the $Y_k$: it
neither assumes a normal law, nor a finite fourth moment, nor a continuous
distribution. Hypotheses of that kind, and any conclusion needing them, must
be stated separately at their point of use.

A sampling model is a mathematical description of repeated observation. It
does not assert that any physical sequence of measurements satisfies the IID
and second-moment hypotheses, and it attaches no value to $\mu$ or $\sigma^2$
beyond the one supplied by the model.

items.title: Mean vector and covariance matrix of a square-integrable random vector
items.statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), let $m\ge1$, and let
$X=(X_1,\dots,X_m):\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with target
$(\mathbb R^m,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m))$ that is **square-integrable**:
$$E\bigl[|X|^2\bigr]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}E\bigl[X_i^2\bigr]<+\infty ,$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
Its **mean vector** is
$$\mu=E[X]:=\bigl(E[X_1],\dots,E[X_m]\bigr)\in\mathbb R^m ,$$
the coordinates being the expectations of
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Its **covariance matrix** is the
$m\times m$ real matrix of [[def-matrix-space]]
$$\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(X):=\bigl(\Sigma_{ij}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{m},\qquad \Sigma_{ij}:=E\bigl[(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)\bigr]\in\mathbb R .$$
For a random vector $Y$ the entries $\Sigma_{ij}$ are also written
$\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$, and $\Sigma_{ii}=\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$.

### Well-definedness and elementary properties

**Integrability of the entries.** Square-integrability gives
$E[X_i^2]<+\infty$ for each $i$. Since $X$ takes values in a probability
space, the elementary inequality
$$|X_i|\le \tfrac12\bigl(1+X_i^2\bigr)$$
and monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) show that each
$X_i$ is integrable, so $\mu_i=E[X_i]$ is a finite real number
([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Likewise
$$|X_i-\mu_i|\le |X_i|+|\mu_i|\le \tfrac12\bigl(1+X_i^2\bigr)+|\mu_i|,$$
so $X_i-\mu_i$ is square-integrable and integrable. Finally
$$|(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)|\le \tfrac12\bigl((X_i-\mu_i)^2+(X_j-\mu_j)^2\bigr),$$
and the right-hand side is integrable by additivity, monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]],
[[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence every
$\Sigma_{ij}$ is a finite real number.

**Symmetry.** For all $i,j$ the real numbers $(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)$ and
$(X_j-\mu_j)(X_i-\mu_i)$ are equal pointwise, so $\Sigma_{ij}=\Sigma_{ji}$;
thus $\Sigma^{\mathsf T}=\Sigma$.

**Positive semidefiniteness.** Let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The
random variable $W:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ is a finite linear combination of
square-integrable random variables, hence square-integrable, and bilinearity
of covariance ([[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]])
gives
$$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\sum_{i,j=1}^{m}z_iz_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) =\operatorname{Cov}(W,W)=\operatorname{Var}(W) =E\bigl[(W-E[W])^2\bigr]\ge0 ,$$
the inequality holding because $(W-E[W])^2\ge0$ pointwise and expectation is
monotone ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]). In
particular $z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=0$ exactly when $W$ is almost surely
constant, so $\Sigma$ is positive definite exactly when for every $z\neq0$
the random variable $\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ fails to be almost surely
constant.

No independence hypothesis is used anywhere in this definition; $\Sigma$
records the pairwise covariances of the coordinates.

items.title: The covariance of the linearization is $A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T}$
items.statement:
Let $m,d\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $\mu\in U$, and let
$h:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel measurable and totally differentiable at $\mu$
with total derivative $A:=Dh(\mu):\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d$
([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]); for instance this
holds when $h$ is $C^1$ on $U$, since continuous maps have Borel preimages of
Borel sets ([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). Let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with values in $U$,
square-integrable with mean vector $E[X]=\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$
([[def-cm-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]]), and define the
**linearization**
$$T:U\longrightarrow\mathbb R^d,\qquad T(x):=h(\mu)+A(x-\mu).$$
Then $T\circ X$ is a random element of $\mathbb R^d$, its mean vector is
$$E\bigl[T(X)\bigr]=h(\mu),$$
and its covariance matrix is
$$\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(T(X)\bigr)=A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T},$$
where $A$ is identified with its Jacobian matrix
$\bigl(\partial_jh_i(\mu)\bigr)_{i,j}$ and $A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T}$ is the
matrix product of [[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]] in the matrix space of
[[def-matrix-space]].

items.title: A uniform Hessian bound controls the second-order Taylor remainder
items.statement:
Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex
([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]), let $h:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class
$C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and let $B\in[0,+\infty)$
satisfy
$$\bigl\lVert H_h(x)\bigr\rVert\le B\qquad\text{for every }x\in U,$$
where $H_h(x)$ is the Hessian of $h$ at $x$
([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]) and $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ is the
operator norm on the finite-dimensional inner-product space of real
$m\times m$ matrices ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]).
Then for all $\mu,y\in U$,
$$\bigl\lvert h(y)-h(\mu)-\nabla h(\mu)\cdot(y-\mu)\bigr\rvert \le\frac{B}{2}\,\lvert y-\mu\rvert^2 ,$$
where $\nabla h(\mu)\cdot(y-\mu)$ is the Euclidean pairing
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

references.title: JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data — Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (BIPM), clause 5.1.2, note to equation (10), on higher-order Taylor terms for significant nonlinearity
K. Bryan, Taylor's Theorem in One and Several Variables (Rose-Hulman MA 433 lecture notes), the second-order case in n dimensions (equation (8)) and its proof (equations (9)-(10))

items.title: Mean and mean-square bounds for the second-order linearization error
items.statement:
Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, let $h:U\to\mathbb R$
be of class $C^2$, and let $B\in[0,+\infty)$ satisfy
$\lVert H_h(x)\rVert\le B$ for every $x\in U$
([[lem-cm-uniform-second-order-remainder-bound]]). Let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with $X(\omega)\in U$ for every
$\omega$, with $E[X]=\mu\in U$ and $E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^2<+\infty$, and put
$$R:=h(X)-h(\mu)-\nabla h(\mu)\cdot(X-\mu).$$
Then $R$ is integrable and
$$\lvert E[R]\rvert\le E\lvert R\rvert \le\frac{B}{2}\,E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^2 .$$
If moreover $E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^4<+\infty$, then $R^2$ is integrable and
$$E\bigl[R^2\bigr]\le\frac{B^2}{4}\,E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^4 .$$

references.title: JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data — Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (BIPM), clause 5.1.2, note to equation (10), and clause H.1 on higher-order terms in the presence of significant nonlinearity
L. Wasserman, All of Statistics: A Concise Course in Statistical Inference (Springer, 2004), Section 5.5 (the delta method as a linear approximation); full text copy at the cited URL

items.title: Statistical tests, rejection regions, power functions and size
items.statement:
Let $(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space, the **data space**
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]); let $\Theta$ be a nonempty
set, the **parameter set**; let $(\mathbb P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a
family of probability measures on $(S,\mathcal S)$
([[def-probability-measure]]), the **model family**; and let $\Theta_0$ be a
nonempty subset of $\Theta$, the **null set**. A **test** of the null set
$\Theta_0$ within the family $(\mathbb P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a set
$R\in\mathcal S$, the **rejection region**; the test *rejects* the null set on
the event that the datum $s\in S$ lies in $R$, and *retains* it otherwise.

The **power function** of the test is
$$\beta:\Theta\longrightarrow[0,1],\qquad \beta(\theta):=\mathbb P_\theta(R),$$
and the **size** of the test is
$$\alpha:=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta)\in[0,1].$$
The test has **level** $\alpha'$ when its size is at most $\alpha'$; the
smallest such $\alpha'$ is the size.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For each $\theta$ the value $\mathbb P_\theta(R)$ is defined because
$R\in\mathcal S$ and $\mathbb P_\theta$ is a measure on $\mathcal S$. The set
$\{\beta(\theta):\theta\in\Theta_0\}$ is nonempty because $\Theta_0\neq
\emptyset$, and it is bounded above by $1$; the least-upper-bound property of
the complete ordered field of reals ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) therefore
supplies its supremum $\alpha\in[0,1]$, uniquely by [[def-complete-ordered-field]].
The size is computed from the null set alone; no alternative set
$\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$, no prior distribution on $\Theta$, and no observed
datum enter its definition.

The rejection region, the family $(\mathbb P_\theta)$ and the null set are
data of the test, not consequences of it. Changing any of them changes
$\beta$ and $\alpha$; a statement that a test has a given size is a statement
about the specified triple $(S,\mathcal S,\{\mathbb P_\theta\})$, the
specified $\Theta_0$ and the specified $R$.
items.strategy: Definition with explicit well-definedness and convention paragraphs; no proof supplied.

references.title: L. Wasserman, All of Statistics: A Concise Course in Statistical Inference (Springer, 2004), Definitions 10.1 and 10.4 and Section 10.1 (rejection regions); full text copy at the cited URL

items.title: Confidence sets and their coverage level
items.statement:
Let $(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space, the **data space**
([[def-measurable-space]]), let $\Theta$ be a nonempty set, the **parameter
set**, and let $(\mathbb P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a family of
probability measures on $(S,\mathcal S)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Write
$2^{\Theta}$ for the power set of $\Theta$. A **confidence set** for
$\Theta$ is a map
$$C:S\longrightarrow 2^{\Theta},\qquad s\longmapsto C(s),$$
such that for every $\theta\in\Theta$ the set
$$\{s\in S:\theta\in C(s)\}$$
is an element of $\mathcal S$. The **coverage of $C$ at $\theta$** is
$$\gamma(\theta):=\mathbb P_\theta\bigl(\theta\in C\bigr),$$
and $C$ has **coverage level** $1-\alpha$ when
$$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\gamma(\theta)\ge1-\alpha .$$

### Well-definedness and conventions

The measurability requirement is exactly what makes each $\gamma(\theta)$
defined, since $\{\theta\in C\}$ is then an event in $\mathcal S$. The family
$\{\gamma(\theta):\theta\in\Theta\}$ is nonempty and bounded below by $0$, so
its infimum exists in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-infimum-property]], is unique by
[[lem-sup-unique]], and equals $\inf_\theta\gamma(\theta)$ as written
([[def-infimum]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

The level is a property of the family $(\mathbb P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$
and of the map $C$; it is an infimum of probabilities of the events
$\theta\in C$, calculated before the datum is observed. It contains no
distribution on $\Theta$ and no conditional probability given the datum; a
data-dependent reading requires further structure that is not part of this
definition.
items.strategy: Definition with explicit well-definedness and convention paragraphs; no proof supplied.

items.title: Likelihood functions for a dominated parametric family
items.statement:
Let $(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space, the **data space**
([[def-measurable-space]]), let $\nu$ be a measure on it ([[def-measure]]),
let $\Theta$ be a nonempty set, the **parameter set**, and let
$$\theta\longmapsto p_\theta,\qquad p_\theta:S\to[0,+\infty],$$
be a family of measurable functions
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]) such that
$$\int_S p_\theta\,d\nu=1\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta$$
([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]). Each $p_\theta$ is the **density**
of a probability measure $\mathbb P_\theta$ with respect to $\nu$,
$$\mathbb P_\theta(A)=\int_A p_\theta\,d\nu,\qquad A\in\mathcal S$$
([[def-measure-with-density]]); the fixed measure $\nu$ is the **dominating
measure** of the family.

For an observed datum $s\in S$ the **likelihood function** is
$$L_s:\Theta\longrightarrow[0,+\infty],\qquad L_s(\theta):=p_\theta(s),$$
and the **log-likelihood function** is
$$\ell_s:\Theta\longrightarrow[-\infty,+\infty],\qquad \ell_s(\theta):=\begin{cases}\log L_s(\theta),&L_s(\theta)>0,\\ -\infty,&L_s(\theta)=0.\end{cases}$$

### Well-definedness and conventions

For fixed $s$ the value $p_\theta(s)$ is a well-defined element of
$[0,+\infty]$ for each $\theta$, so $L_s$ and $\ell_s$ are defined as
functions on $\Theta$; no measurability or integrability in $\theta$ is
asserted, and no topology on $\Theta$ is assumed. The densities $p_\theta$
and the dominating measure $\nu$ are data of the model: a likelihood claim
must name the pair $(\nu,(p_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ it uses, since the
same family of probability measures can be represented by different pairs.

The value $L_s(\theta)$ is the density of the observed datum under the
parameter $\theta$; it is not a probability of the parameter value $\theta$,
and no distribution on $\Theta$ is part of this definition.

items.title: Symbolic two-input propagation of a period–length model
items.statement:
Consider the model function
$$h:\mathbb R^2\supseteq U\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad h(T,l):=\frac{4\pi^2l}{T^2},\qquad U:=\{(T,l)\in\mathbb R^2:T>0\},$$
where $T$ represents a duration and $l$ a length in an adopted unit
convention; the definition here is purely formal and no physical model,
period, length or measurement is asserted. The set $U$ is open and convex in
$\mathbb R^2$, and $h$ is $C^\infty$ there. Fix a nominal input
$\mu=(T_0,l_0)\in U$ with $T_0>0$, and let $(T,l):\Omega\to U$ be a
square-integrable random vector with
$$E[(T,l)]=(T_0,l_0),\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(T,l)=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_T^2&\sigma_{Tl}\\ \sigma_{Tl}&\sigma_l^2\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then the linearization of $h$ at $\mu$ has slope
$$Dh(\mu)=\Bigl(-\frac{8\pi^2l_0}{T_0^3},\ \frac{4\pi^2}{T_0^2}\Bigr),$$
and the propagated covariance of the linearization is the $1\times1$ matrix
$$Dh(\mu)\operatorname{Cov}(T,l)Dh(\mu)^{\mathsf T} =\frac{64\pi^4l_0^2}{T_0^{6}}\,\sigma_T^2 -\frac{64\pi^4l_0}{T_0^{5}}\,\sigma_{Tl} +\frac{16\pi^4}{T_0^{4}}\,\sigma_l^2 .$$
This is a symbolic computation in a declared model; it neither supplies
values for $T_0,l_0,\sigma_T^2,\sigma_{Tl},\sigma_l^2$ nor asserts that any
apparatus realizes the model. A physical reading in which $T$ is a period and
$l$ a length, and in which a pendulum protocol with a small-angle model is
used to estimate a gravitational parameter, belongs to a separate physical
item that states the protocol, the small-angle idealization and its
remaining error; no such reading is made here.

references.title: JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data — Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (BIPM), clauses 5.1.2–5.1.3 and example H.5.2 (period of a pendulum model) on sensitivity coefficients

items.title: Exact variance against propagated variance for a nonlinear observation map
items.statement:
Let $\Omega=\{\omega_0,\omega_1,\omega_2\}$ carry the weights
$w(\omega_0)=1/2$, $w(\omega_1)=w(\omega_2)=1/4$, let
$$Y:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad Y(\omega_0)=0,\quad Y(\omega_1)=1,\quad Y(\omega_2)=3,$$
and let $h(y):=y^2$ on the open convex set $U=(-1,4)$, which contains the
three values of $Y$. Then $h$ is $C^2$ with constant Hessian $H_h(x)=(2)$ and
operator norm $B=2$, the mean is $\mu=E[Y]=1\in U$, and
$$E[Y^2]=\frac52,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\frac32,\qquad E[Y^4]=\frac{41}{2},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(h(Y)) =\frac{41}{2}-\Bigl(\frac52\Bigr)^2=\frac{57}{4}.$$
The linearization $T(y)=h(1)+h'(1)(y-1)=1+2(y-1)$ has variance
$$h'(1)^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)=4\cdot\frac32=6 =\frac{24}{4}\neq\frac{57}{4}=\operatorname{Var}(h(Y)),$$
so the propagated variance is not the exact variance of $h(Y)$. The
linearization error $R=h(Y)-T(Y)=(Y-1)^2$ satisfies
$$E[R]=\frac32=\frac{B}{2}E\bigl[(Y-1)^2\bigr],\qquad E\bigl[R^2\bigr]=\frac92=\frac{B^2}{4}E\bigl[(Y-1)^4\bigr],$$
so both displayed bounds of
[[cor-cm-linearization-error-bounds]] are attained in this example. The
example contains no measured quantity and asserts no physical model.

references.title: JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data — Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (BIPM), clause 5.1.2, note to equation (10), on higher-order terms when the nonlinearity of the model function is significant

items.title: Finite check of the IID sample-mean variance and Chebyshev bound
items.statement:
Let $\Omega=\{(\sigma_1,\sigma_2):\sigma_1,\sigma_2\in\{-1,1\}\}$ be the uniform
finite probability space with four outcomes of weight $1/4$, and let
$$X_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2):=\sigma_1,\qquad X_2(\sigma_1,\sigma_2):=\sigma_2 .$$
Then $(X_1,X_2)$ is an IID family with $\mu=E[X_1]=0$ and
$\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=1$; the sample mean
$\overline X=(X_1+X_2)/2$ takes the values $-1,0,1$ with probabilities
$1/4,1/2,1/4$ respectively. The exact second moment and the Chebyshev bound
of [[cor-iid-finite-variance-weak-law]] read
$$E\bigl\lvert\overline X\bigr\rvert^2=\frac12=\frac{\sigma^2}{2},\qquad \mathbb P\bigl(\lvert\overline X\rvert\ge1\bigr)=\frac12 =\frac{\sigma^2}{2\cdot1^2},$$
so the bound is attained at $a=1$, while
$$\mathbb P\Bigl(\lvert\overline X\rvert\ge\frac12\Bigr)=\frac12 \le2=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\cdot(1/2)^2}$$
is strict. This is a finite check inside the stated model; it evaluates no
measurement and estimates no physical quantity.

references.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Section 2.2.1 (the variance of a sum of independent variables and the Chebyshev bound for the i.i.d. sample mean)

items.title: Equality and strictness in the uniform second-order remainder bound
items.statement:
Two explicit one-variable cases of
[[lem-cm-uniform-second-order-remainder-bound]].

**A quadratic on an interval.** Let $h(y):=y^2$ on the open convex set
$U=(-1,3)$ and fix $\mu=1$. Then $h$ is $C^2$ with constant Hessian $(2)$, so
$\lVert H_h(y)\rVert=2$ for every $y\in U$ and $B=2$ is the sharp constant.
For every $y\in U$,
$$h(y)-h(1)-h'(1)(y-1)=y^2-1-2(y-1)=(y-1)^2 =\frac{B}{2}\lvert y-1\rvert^2,$$
so the inequality of the lemma is an equality for every $y\in U$.

**A cubic on an interval.** Let $g(y):=y^3$ on the open convex set
$V=(-1,2)$ and fix $\mu=1/2$. Then $g$ is $C^2$ with Hessian $(6y)$, and
$\lVert H_g(y)\rVert=\lvert6y\rvert\le12$ on $V$, so $B=12$ is an admissible
constant. At $y=1$,
$$g(1)-g\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)-g'\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)\Bigl(1-\frac12\Bigr) =1-\frac18-\frac34\cdot\frac12=\frac12 \le\frac{12}{2}\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^2=\frac32 ,$$
so the bound holds strictly at this point. Both computations are formal and
assert nothing beyond the stated intervals.

references.title: K. Bryan, Taylor's Theorem in One and Several Variables (Rose-Hulman MA 433 lecture notes), the second-order case in n dimensions (equation (8)) and the Hessian matrix form 1/2 (x-a)^T H(b) (x-a)

items.title: Coverage level is not the posterior probability of the realized confidence set
items.statement:
Statement refuted: "if $C$ is a confidence set of level $1-\alpha$ for a
family $(\mathbb P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ and $\pi$ is any probability
distribution on $\Theta$ for which the conditional law of $\theta$ given the
datum $s$ exists, then the conditional probability that $\theta\in C(s)$
given $s$ equals $1-\alpha$"
([[def-cm-confidence-set-and-coverage]]).

references.title: L. Wasserman, All of Statistics: A Concise Course in Statistical Inference (Springer, 2004), Example 6.14 (after Berger and Wolpert, 1984) and the warning in Section 6.3.2; full text copy at the cited URL

S. Greenland, S. J. Senn, K. J. Rothman, J. B. Carlin, C. Poole, S. N. Goodman and D. G. Altman, 'Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations', European Journal of Epidemiology 31 (2016), 337–350

items.title: The propagated covariance is not the exact covariance of a nonlinear observation map
items.statement:
Statement refuted: "if $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ is open and convex, $h:U\to\mathbb R$
is $C^2$, $X:\Omega\to U$ is square-integrable with $E[X]=\mu\in U$, and
$\Sigma$ is its covariance matrix, then
$\operatorname{Cov}(h(X))=Dh(\mu)\Sigma Dh(\mu)^{\mathsf T}$, that is,
$\operatorname{Var}(h(X))=h'(\mu)^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$"
([[lem-cm-linearized-propagation-of-covariance]]).

references.title: JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data — Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (BIPM), clause 5.1.2, note to equation (10), on the first-order character of the propagated variance
